idea.why: Genuine multi-agent decomposition matching the brief, with concerns cleanly separated and none smeared across redundant nodes. The soft spot is that the final artefact is produced freehand rather than from a structured intermediate, so sorting and layout are fused into a single non-deterministic step.

structure.why: Every node type is the right one, with pre-scoped windows on both tools and one shared model serving all three agents rather than three copies. The visible gap is that no templating node is used for the markup, leaving a purpose-built rendering job to prose instructions in a system message.

connections.why: Wiring matches the real dependencies exactly. The two independent fetches are not serialised into a main chain; they hang off the orchestrator as tool branches, each with its own data tool beneath it. No artificial merge, no dangling branch, nothing unreachable.

answer.why: End to end it does what was asked, with anti-hallucination and empty-section rules, the right instinct for real data. What weakens it is delivery robustness: output is piped straight into the mail body with no guard, and the simple fetch mode returns snippets only, so the per-message summary is thinner than the prompt implies.

appraisal: The shape a knowledgeable user would reach for: a root agent with two tool-exposed specialists, each owning exactly one purpose-built Google tool, one shared model, and a two-hop main chain that does not pretend independent fetches are sequential. The prompts are unusually disciplined, with explicit urgency criteria, chronological ordering, free-block detection, and hard instructions never to invent items. Where it slips is the last mile: the dashboard is generated freehand and piped unguarded into the send, so layout drifts run to run and one malformed generation produces an unreadable briefing, while the simple fetch mode starves the summariser of body text. The first change is structured output rendered through a template node.
